extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and reporters learning courtroom and legal news writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for writing news stories about criminal and civil court proceedings, judicial decisions, and related human-interest outcomes. Focuses on what details to include, tone to adopt, and how to present testimony, legal reasoning, and background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain appropriate tone in court reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Murder trials are not supposed to be humorous affairs and Justices bend severe glances upon flippant witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the gravity of the proceedings and avoid trivializing them; if a witness is flippant or amusing, note the effect on the court (e.g., 'schepps somehow dissipated the gravity of the proceedings and lightened the black tale of crime') but balance such color with respect for the seriousness of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe witness character and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the witness's demeanor and appearance: childlike vanity, mannerisms, clothing and gestures (e.g., 'his childlike vanity', 'sharp eyes squinted behind his nose glasses', 'he wore a blue suit, a black four-in-hand tie').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid but factual descriptions to humanize participants and give readers a sense of personality and courtroom dynamics; include dress, gestures, facial expressions, and changes in demeanor over the course of testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report direct testimony and verbatim quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the substance of testimony and direct quotations from witnesses and parties (e.g., 'Don't mind anything. I'll fix it all right. They have to prove who killed Rosenthal before they can convict any one.' ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Q. and A. transcripts or verbatim quotes where possible to convey exact statements; reproduce exchanges that are central to the case and that illuminate intent, admissions, or defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Q&A format where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting testimony in a Q. A. format (question and answer) to show the flow of examination and exact exchanges between counsel and witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, preserve short Q/A blocks to demonstrate how facts were elicited and to show confrontations between counsel and witnesses; this helps readers follow evidentiary development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include procedural details of the trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Report which witnesses were called, adjournments, time taken for examinations, and courtroom rulings (e.g., 'Mr. Moss had no further questions... the direct examination ended at 11:02 A.M., having occupied only twenty-seven minutes', 'There was no time left for the long examination that would be necessary and Justice Goff rather reluctantly consented to adjournment.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document courtroom procedure and pacing (who testified, what was planned but not done, lengths of examinations) to convey the conduct of the trial and why coverage proceeded as it did.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide precise chronological and locational details
rubrics_metrics.description: Give times, streets, addresses and sequence of events (e.g., 'riding in an auto with a chauffeur at Sixth avenue and Forty-sixth street at 1:30 o'clock A.M.', 'Seventh avenue and 145th street').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete time/place information anchors narrative credibility and helps readers reconstruct events; include travel, meetings, and where and when key acts occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize defense and prosecution strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the efforts and focal points of counsel (e.g., 'Lieut. Becker's chief counsel concentrated his efforts to make Schepps say something that would indicate that he knew Rosenthal was to be murdered... It was an attack of the utmost importance to the defence.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify what each side is trying to prove or discredit, the significance of particular lines of questioning, and tactical moves such as introducing witnesses from other locations to impeach credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide background and history of persons involved
rubrics_metrics.description: Include relevant personal, criminal and civil histories of defendants or principals (e.g., extensive history of Koch's aliases, prior suits and convictions; Florence Lemoine's past employment and earnings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual biographies help explain motives, patterns of behavior, credibility, and potential penalties; include prior convictions, aliases, employment, family status and other salient history.

rubrics_metrics.name: State legal holdings and reasoning when reporting decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the court's holding and the legal test or reasoning used (e.g., the Appellate Division reversed because acts were 'not committed in furtherance of the master's business' and quoted the test: 'If a servant goes outside of his employment... the master is not responsible').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering judicial opinions, summarize the rule of law, the court's application, and, where useful, include short quoted passages from the opinion to capture the doctrinal test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain practical implications of legal rulings
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how a ruling affects people locally and broadly (e.g., Supreme Court decision on expatriation 'means... a woman born in California... automatically relinquishes her citizenship... the moment she becomes the wife of a foreigner').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate legal holdings into plain-language consequences for affected populations and name specific groups or examples impacted by the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote official legal opinions and interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Include text from formal opinions or advisory opinions (e.g., Attorney General F. L. Gilbert: 'It seems to me that the plain spirit, intent and purpose of the law in question was to establish a maximum passenger rate...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct quotations from judges, appellate opinions, or attorneys-general to convey authoritative legal interpretations and to preserve nuance of statutory interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight human-interest outcomes and impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the human consequences: victims' conditions, economic losses, earnings, and emotional states (e.g., Florence Lemoine's paralysis and loss of stage career; Koch spending winnings on liquor; the Kaminoka Strumolova funeral mistake and loss of two hundred dollars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement legal and procedural reporting with the human story to show stakes and societal effects; include earnings, health, family circumstances and quotes illustrating impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report immediate outcomes and next steps
rubrics_metrics.description: State verdicts, sentencing intentions, restorations, releases and forthcoming proceedings (e.g., 'Koch will be brought before Judge Fesler later for sentence', 'He was freed from the asylum', 'The window of the murdered gambler will be the first witness to-day').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear what decisions were reached and what will happen next in the case so readers understand resolution and anticipate follow-up coverage.
